passage: Noa's slides about coral reefs were packed with full sentences. Standing beside the screen in the Lisbon classroom, Noa kept both eyes on it and read every slide word for word in a flat voice, because looking at faces made her stomach twist. Halfway through, a boy yawned. Priscila, in the front row, was already reading ahead. When Noa reached the last slide, the silence was not interest but boredom. Afterwards Priscila said, "I could have read it myself. Tell me what you'd say if you were explaining reefs at lunch." The next day Noa used three words per slide and spoke to Priscila. This time, people asked questions.

qa.q: Who was already reading ahead on the screen?
qa.a: Priscila, in the front row, was already reading ahead.

qa.q: Why did Noa keep both eyes on the screen and read every slide word for word?
qa.a: Noa was nervous, because looking at faces made her stomach twist, so the screen felt safe.

qa.q: What change made the next presentation better?
qa.a: Noa used three words per slide and spoke to Priscila as if explaining reefs at lunch, so people asked questions.

qa.q: How did Priscila see the first presentation?
qa.a: Priscila found it unnecessary and dull, since the audience could have read the slides themselves. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teenager reading slides word for word to cope with nerves and losing the audience.

passage: In the school computer lab, Eshaan clicked to his fourth slide and read it out exactly as written: "Household water usage has increased over the last ten years." His voice was quick and his eyes stayed on the projector screen. The pencils in the room stopped moving. Sunaina Ma'am, at the back with the marking sheet, wrote one note: "eyes on the slide, not us." After the bell she said, "Your slides are good. Now keep the sentences in your head, not on the wall. What is the one thing you want us to remember?" Eshaan thought. "That a running tap while brushing wastes a bucket." "Then show a bucket and say that." In the next lesson he showed the bucket, said one sentence and looked at people. Hands went up.

qa.q: What did Sunaina Ma'am write on the marking sheet?
qa.a: She wrote: "eyes on the slide, not us."

qa.q: Why might Eshaan have read the slides word for word?
qa.a: Eshaan was probably nervous, and reading felt safe and kept him from forgetting.

qa.q: What did Eshaan change for the next lesson?
qa.a: He showed one picture of a bucket, said one sentence aloud and looked at his classmates.

qa.q: How might the class have felt when their pencils stopped moving?
qa.a: Bored and disengaged, since the class could have read the slide themselves.

grounding: Shows a teenager reading slides aloud to feel safe and a teacher's nudge toward speaking to the audience.

passage:
The Class Ten room at the government school in Rajgarh had one borrowed projector, a sheet pinned to the wall and a fan that kept stopping. Leela's group was presenting on solar water pumps.
Leela had made the slides herself, and she had put everything on them: twelve lines per slide, small letters. When it was her turn, she turned to face the sheet and read. Her voice was steady, but her back was to the class.
By the third slide, the boys at the back were drawing on each other's hands. Two girls whispered. Irfan sir tapped his pen.
Then the power cut off. The sheet went blank. Leela stood there, heart thumping. Irfan sir said, "Just tell us. How does the pump work?"
She turned around. She talked about her uncle's farm and the pump he got last year, how the water came on at noon. The back row stopped drawing. When the power came back, she didn't turn to the screen again.

qa.q: How many lines did Leela put on each slide?
qa.a: Twelve lines per slide, small letters.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when the power cut off?
qa.a: Leela felt a jolt of fear, standing there with her heart thumping when the slides vanished.

qa.q: What does the power cut show about reading from slides?
qa.a: Without the screen, Leela spoke to the class and they listened, which shows reading slides was safe for her but lost the audience.

qa.q: How might Irfan sir see Leela's first few slides?
qa.a: Irfan sir was probably restless and concerned, tapping his pen as the class drifted while Leela read with her back to them.

grounding: Shows a teenager who reads full slides with her back to the class until a power cut forces her to talk, and the audience returns.

passage:
In Vancouver, Chen's Grade Nine science presentation on honeybees had eighteen slides. Each one was packed with sentences he had copied from his notes.
He stood beside the screen, clicker in hand, and read. He did not look up once. Reading felt safe; if the words were there, he couldn't go blank.
From his seat, Kofi watched the room. By slide seven, two people had their heads on their desks. Kofi himself had read ahead and was already on slide nine in his head.
Afterwards, Ms Laurent's feedback note said: "Excellent research. But I could read it myself. What do YOU think is the most surprising thing about bees?" Chen stared at the question. He knew the answer: that they dance to show each other where flowers are. It wasn't on any slide.
For the next project, he put one picture per slide and a few words. He practised telling it to his mom at dinner.

qa.q: How many slides did Chen's presentation have?
qa.a: It had eighteen slides.

qa.q: Why did Chen read every slide without looking up?
qa.a: Chen felt nervous about going blank, and reading felt safe because the words were there.

qa.q: What did Chen change for the next project, and why does it help?
qa.a: One picture and a few words per slide, practised aloud at dinner, so he has to talk to people rather than read to them.

qa.q: What was the presentation like for Kofi?
qa.a: Kofi was bored and had read ahead to slide nine, watching others put their heads on their desks.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who reads packed slides to cope with nerves, losing an audience that could read them faster.

passage: At the district science centre's student day, Ritu's turn came after lunch, when the hall was warm and sleepy. Her topic was solar cookers, and she had twelve slides crowded with full sentences. She stood half-turned to the screen and read: "A solar cooker is a device which uses the energy of direct sunlight to heat and cook food." Click. Next slide. Read. She didn't look at the audience once; looking at them made her throat close. From the third row, Reena watched a father check his phone, two boys whisper, a grandmother nod off. Ritu finished and got polite clapping. Outside, by the water cooler, Reena said carefully, "The pictures were great. But you read every word. People could've read it themselves." Ritu's face went tight. "If I look away from the screen, I'll forget everything." "Then put three words on each slide," Reena said, "and look at me. I'll nod." Ritu said nothing, but she didn't walk away.

qa.q: How many slides did Ritu have?
qa.a: Twelve slides.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when Reena mentioned reading every word?
qa.a: Ritu felt stung and defensive, her face going tight, because reading was how she coped with her fear of forgetting.

qa.q: What small step did Reena suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Put three words on each slide and look at Reena, so Ritu has a prompt but talks to people, with a friendly nodding face to steady her.

qa.q: What was the talk like for the audience, as Reena saw it?
qa.a: They drifted away: a father checked his phone, two boys whispered and a grandmother nodded off, since everything was already written on the screen.

grounding: Shows a teenager who reads each slide word for word to cope with nerves and loses the audience, who could have read it themselves.
